steps.scene: A quiet residential crossroads. There are no signs, no give-way lines and no markings on any of the four roads.

options.text: You do, because your road is wider
No-one — you both have to be sure before you go
Whoever gets there first

question.explanation: At an unmarked crossroads nobody has priority. Slow right down, look both ways, and be ready to give way.

steps.title: Keep the box clear
steps.body: Enter a yellow box junction only when your exit road is clear, so you can drive straight across without stopping in it.

question.prompt: Traffic is queuing on the far side of a yellow box junction. When can you drive into the box?

options.text: As soon as the lights turn green
When your exit road is clear
Whenever the traffic ahead is queuing slowly

question.explanation: The box exists to keep the junction flowing. If you would have to stop inside it, wait outside it.

a.label: Going straight on
a.body: Never enter the box until your exit is clear. Slow queueing traffic is not an exception.

b.label: Turning right
b.body: You may wait in the box when the only thing stopping you is oncoming traffic.

question.prompt: You're turning right and oncoming traffic is holding you up. What may you do?

options.text: Wait in the box, as long as your exit is clear
Nothing — you may never stop inside a box junction
Reverse back out of the box

question.explanation: The right-turn wait is the one exception to keeping the box clear — and your exit still has to be clear.

steps.scene: You're turning right at a crossroads. A driver coming the other way is turning right too, and you meet in the middle.

question.prompt: Why is it usually better to pass behind each other?

options.text: It gets both of you through more quickly
You each get a clearer view of the traffic coming towards you
Once you've started to turn, oncoming traffic must wait for you

question.explanation: Passing behind each other keeps your view along the road open. Nose to nose, you each hide what the other needs to see.

steps.title: Whose side is blocked?
steps.body: When parked cars or roadworks block your side of the road, the gap belongs to oncoming traffic. Wait until it's clear.

question.prompt: Parked cars block your side and a car is coming the other way. What do you do?

options.text: Give way — the obstruction is on your side
Keep going, because you reached the gap first
Flash your headlights and drive through

question.explanation: The obstruction is yours to deal with, so the road is theirs. Hold back where you can see and be seen.

steps.scene: You're waiting to turn right onto a dual carriageway. The gap in the central reservation is shorter than your car.

options.text: Wait until both carriageways are clear, then cross in one go
Cross to the gap and wait there for the far side to clear
Turn left and make a U-turn further along

question.explanation: If your car would stick out into a live lane, treat it as one crossing and go only when both directions are clear.

steps.wrongBelief: A driver flashing their headlights at a junction is telling you it's safe to pull out.

question.prompt: What does a flash of headlights actually tell you?

options.text: Come out — the way is clear
Only that someone is there — the decision is still yours
That the driver is annoyed with you

question.explanation: Flashing headlights means the same as the horn: 'I am here.' It is never a signal that the road is safe.

steps.repairNote: A flash only says someone is there. Whether it's safe to emerge is still your judgement, not theirs.
